Where to send what

Same inbox either way — this just helps it get to the right person faster.

  • Sales and scoping

    What you sell, how many people, what is breaking. You will get a written scope and a number, usually within one business day.

  • Support, if you are already a customer

    By email, and by phone on the number in your agreement. Something that has stopped your business working gets looked at the same day.

  • Security

    Vulnerability reports and due-diligence questionnaires. Acknowledged within one business day. The security page says what is built and what is not.

  • Privacy and data requests

    Access, correction, erasure, or withdrawing consent. Answered within thirty days, and you do not need a lawyer, a format or a reason.

You do not need us if

This is the section most vendors leave out, and it is the one that saves everyone the most time. If you recognise yourself here, we will tell you the same thing on a call — so read it first and keep your afternoon.

  • You are under ten people in one location selling one product line. Tally and a good spreadsheet are genuinely fine, and a system will cost you more in discipline than it returns.
  • Nothing is actually broken. "We should probably modernise" is not a reason, and a project without a specific problem behind it is the kind that gets abandoned in month four.
  • You need one thing, not a system. If the real problem is invoicing, buy invoicing software. We would rather point you at one than sell you a platform for it.
  • Your procurement requires SOC 2 or ISO 27001 today. We do not have either, will not for a while, and would fail your review — better to know now.
  • You want it live in two weeks. Data migration alone rarely fits in two weeks, and we will not pretend otherwise to win the work.

The things people are actually thinking

We tried this before and it failed.

Most businesses of your size have. It usually failed for one of three reasons: the data going in was dirty and nobody said so; the rollout went to everybody at once instead of one team; or the person who wanted it left. None of those are software problems, which is why the process page spends more time on them than on features. Tell us what happened last time — it is the most useful thing you can tell us.

Our accountant will not like it.

Ask them what they actually need, then send us the list. In our experience they want three things: clean documents, a reliable export, and not being surprised. Ordence does not replace your CA or file your returns, and the export is designed for someone who has to work with it rather than admire it.

What if the person who sets it up leaves?

Yours or ours. If it is yours: everything is configuration rather than tribal knowledge, and we write down what was decided and why. If it is ours — that is a fair question about a small company and the FAQ answers it directly rather than reassuringly.

How do we know you will still be here in two years?

You do not, and neither does any vendor who tells you otherwise. What you can check is what happens if we are not: your data exports in open formats, at any time, without asking, and the terms say so. That is the only promise on this subject worth anything.

What to expect

A person reads it, usually the same day. If the answer needs thought you will get an acknowledgement first rather than silence, and you will not be handed between three people who each ask you to explain it again.

We are a small team, which means occasionally you will wait a few hours longer than you would from a company with a follow-the-sun desk. It also means the person replying can actually change the thing you are asking about.
